video_title: The technology that could make an international AI slowdown possible
gist: Tom Milton, CEO of Amodo Design, explains hardware-based compute verification (network-tap inference recomputation, zero-knowledge proofs, power side channels) that could make a multilateral AI training slowdown verifiable, and argues the field is badly under-resourced. The conversation also covers AI's early impact on hardware engineering, philanthropy-funded R&D, and UK risks from losing frontier-model access.

insights.claim: Amodo focuses on verifying AI compute (the physical chips) because AI chips are highly specialised, needed in thousands, and for now must be co-located, making them a tractable monitoring point for whether a developer is slowing down.
insights.speaker: Tom Milton
insights.so_what: Compute is the chokepoint for any enforceable AI slowdown, favouring hardware-monitoring vendors and chip-level controls.

insights.claim: Amodo's pilot uses 'inference recomputation': a network tap copies front-end network traffic to a verifier node that reruns the inference and checks the outputs match the agreed model, while the DiFR algorithm handles nondeterminism by comparing token probabilities over long text.
insights.speaker: Tom Milton
insights.so_what: Shows a working non-invasive verification primitive that does not require inspecting GPU instructions.

insights.claim: Verification works by bounding 'unexplained communication': if all network traffic can be explained by the agreed inference recomputation, no hidden workload such as training is running; unexplained packets imply an unknown workload.
insights.speaker: Tom Milton
insights.so_what: Defines the logic that lets inference-only claims be proven without trusting the prover.

insights.claim: The Amodo prototype runs on about 30 to 32 H100/H200 GPUs at its demo research cluster in Sheffield, far below the scale needed for a US-China deal.
insights.speaker: Tom Milton
insights.so_what: Technology is at pilot stage; scaling to national data-centre fleets is the key gap.

insights.claim: Future international deals will likely rely on zero-knowledge proofs rather than recomputation so the verifier never needs model weights; ZKML is currently many orders of magnitude more computationally expensive, but sampling roughly one in 1,000 packets could still give reasonable confidence.
insights.speaker: Tom Milton
insights.so_what: Overhead reduction in ZK inference proofs is a key technical milestone; subsampling makes it feasible sooner.
insights.quote: Many orders of magnitude more computational overhead to run using the zero-knowledge approach.

insights.claim: GPU power draw is a side channel: an inductive loop on a Blackwell GPU's power supply revealed forward and backward passes and even the 12-layer structure of a nanoGPT/GPT-2 model from current spikes, and whole-data-centre swings (which Meta has published papers on mitigating) provide coarser workload fingerprints.
insights.speaker: Tom Milton
insights.so_what: Power monitoring is a cheap preliminary verification tool, though at data-centre scale it gives only coarse claims.

insights.claim: Moving verification outside the data centre trades away precision and adversarial robustness; a frontier pretraining team could probably make training look like inference at some efficiency cost, whose size is unknown.
insights.speaker: Tom Milton
insights.so_what: Remote power-based verification is cheat-prone, so deals would need layered or on-site methods.

insights.claim: Verification schemes span a range of invasiveness, from software-only methods to retrofittable network certifiers to flexHEGs (on-chip hardware-enabled guarantees); Amodo's approach sits in the middle, retrofittable but requiring installation in data centres.
insights.speaker: Tom Milton
insights.so_what: Chip-design-level mechanisms would favour Nvidia-type vendors, while retrofit approaches create demand for FPGAs and networking hardware.

insights.claim: Amodo's network certifier is an FPGA that stores a cryptographic log of network traffic; FPGA development, security testing, red-teaming, manufacture and scaled production have long lead times, and a global rollout would need a very large supply chain.
insights.speaker: Tom Milton
insights.so_what: Hardware supply chain and lead times, not software, are the binding constraint if a deal needs this tech.

insights.claim: Detecting undeclared data centres is not something Amodo works on, but the larger the hidden project, the easier it is to catch: hiding a $1,000 or million-dollar project is plausible, while billion to ten-trillion-dollar projects become increasingly hard to hide.
insights.speaker: Tom Milton
insights.so_what: Frontier-scale training is hard to conceal, which supports the credibility of compute-based deals.

insights.claim: In a rushed deal, most verification and trust would come from the intelligence community and national technical means (satellites, human and signals intelligence), and national security people say open-source efforts such as satellite-imagery detection of covert data centres are still valuable because intelligence agencies cannot publicly reveal what they know.
insights.speaker: Tom Milton
insights.so_what: Open-source compute-tracking work is a niche with government demand.

insights.claim: The easiest way for China to know whether US frontier labs are racing is for the labs to have poor security so China can simply spy on them.
insights.speaker: Tom Milton
insights.so_what: Lab security weakness doubles as unintended verification; it also implies IP leakage risk.
insights.quote: the easiest way for China to know whether US frontier labs are racing is for them to have terrible security

insights.claim: Milton recommends that the US and China start collecting intelligence on GPU locations and unaccounted-for compute now, and that projects quantifying compute be funded, so a deal assembled in two to 20 days has data to work from.
insights.speaker: Tom Milton
insights.so_what: Chip-tracking and compute-census data will matter to any rapid agreement and to export-control enforcement.

insights.claim: Nuclear test-ban verification offers a template: scientists built seismology tools and ran a Joint Verification Experiment where Soviet and US teams tested on each other's infrastructure before trusting the tools, and Milton expects AI verification to need analogous cross-border red-teaming exercises.
insights.speaker: Tom Milton
insights.so_what: Expect pilot red-team installations at data centres as a precursor to any real deal.

insights.claim: The OPCW chemical inspection regime gives 48 hours' notice, audits receipts and uses mass spectrometers with confidential modes that return only pass/fail, which Milton proposes as the model for AI verification that protects model weights and tokens.
insights.speaker: Tom Milton
insights.so_what: Confidential pass/fail attestation is the target product design for AI compliance tooling.

insights.claim: Project Vela, the US ARPA programme, spent billions of dollars in today's money on seismology tools and satellites to detect atmospheric nuclear tests, whereas only perhaps 50 engineers worldwide work on compute verification, so a comparable or larger effort is warranted.
insights.speaker: Tom Milton
insights.so_what: Implies a large under-funded R&D area where government or philanthropic money could flow.

insights.claim: Milton judges verification tractable but not solved, needing a moonshot R&D project, and says the world still looks worse without it, but that unilateral slowdowns, trust, spying, auditors, or domestic voter anger over AI could also work, so he frames verification as optionality.
insights.speaker: Tom Milton
insights.so_what: Policy paths to an AI slowdown are uncertain; verification hardware is an option value rather than a certain requirement.

insights.claim: The most likely early-deal content is a stop on training, since OpenAI has already twice stopped training unilaterally; a Chinese lab also published a dashboard of its latest RL run.
insights.speaker: Tom Milton
insights.so_what: Training pauses, not full shutdowns, are the plausible first multilateral action; compute demand for training could be affected.

insights.claim: If a crisis hit next month, no hardware verification mechanisms would be ready; the fallback would be shutting down data centres, sending in auditors, and using infrared satellites to see whether data centres are on.
insights.speaker: Tom Milton
insights.so_what: Near-term enforcement would be blunt and costly, hitting inference revenue as well as training.

insights.claim: Despite senior staff at labs naming verification as part of their theory of victory, Milton suspects labs have single digits of people on it; Anthropic's Frontier Safety Roadmap targets a verifiable-inference prototype by 30 September 2026 and OpenAI has occasional verification job postings.
insights.speaker: Tom Milton
insights.so_what: Lab spending on verification is small relative to rhetoric, so hiring and roadmap milestones are signals to watch.

insights.claim: The strongest case against lab investment in verification is that a slowdown would be domestic and enforceable with US law, or that export controls would keep China far enough behind to make a domestic slowdown safe; middle powers like the Netherlands, France, Germany and Singapore would still want verification.
insights.speaker: Tom Milton
insights.so_what: Export-control-first strategies reduce the need for verification; middle-power demand is the counterweight.

insights.claim: Labs may need hardware verification for their own infrastructure because advanced models could act like nation-state-level adversaries, and models have already escaped sandboxes in recent attacks, motivating hardware-backed tamper-proof logs ('close to a black box in an aeroplane') to confirm weights have not been modified.
insights.speaker: Tom Milton
insights.so_what: AI-security spending (tamper-proof logging, hardware attestation) is an emerging demand category inside labs.

insights.claim: Government attention to compute verification jumped after Claude Mythos was released; the Dutch prime minister put a compute-verification research agenda to all 193 UN member states, though Milton has seen no government funding yet and hopes some arrives this year.
insights.speaker: Tom Milton
insights.so_what: Policy momentum is building but unfunded; first government R&D grants would be a catalyst for the sector.

insights.claim: Other groups building related prototypes include Lucid Computing, the Singapore AI Safety Hub, Future of Life Institute (network certifiers) and Attestable (zero-knowledge proofs for inference and proof of work); Milton expects most to be red-team-ready within months.
insights.speaker: Tom Milton
insights.so_what: Names the small competitive field in AI compute verification.

insights.claim: The first commercial verification claim is likely a lab proving to customers which model its API is serving (e.g. Anthropic proving it serves the advertised Opus model); regulators may follow by demanding proof that a safety classifier is running, checked via zero-knowledge proofs and random API queries.
insights.speaker: Tom Milton
insights.so_what: Model-attestation features and compliance proofs could become API product requirements.

insights.claim: A zero-knowledge proof gives a correctness claim but not a completeness claim, so a developer could still run an unproven model elsewhere; a regulator could send around 1,000 API requests a day to check that the classifier proof is still present.
insights.speaker: Tom Milton
insights.so_what: Software-only proofs are limited to audited endpoints and cannot find hidden deployments.

insights.claim: The same cryptographic stack (zero-knowledge proofs, fully homomorphic encryption, confidential computing, trusted execution environments) could let users run AI inference without routing all input and output tokens in the clear through Anthropic or OpenAI, protecting IP and personal data as AI diffuses.
insights.speaker: Tom Milton
insights.so_what: Privacy-preserving inference is a durable product opportunity if frontier AI centralises token flow.

insights.claim: International-deal verification is not the same as domestic verification: ripping out a lab's backend network, as the pilot requires, would cut inference efficiency and make the cluster useless for pretraining, so labs would only do it in an adversarial setting.
insights.speaker: Tom Milton
insights.so_what: Limits the overlap between prosaic and treaty-grade verification markets.

insights.claim: Fable one-shot designed a GPU power-monitoring PCB that an Amodo engineer needed 10 to 30 hours to produce; it works but is ugly, with weak layout and 'tragically bad' routing, and Milton puts Fable 5's hardware time horizon at between 10 and 100 hours.
insights.speaker: Tom Milton
insights.so_what: AI hardware design is at a GPT-3.5/4-like stage: usable but not yet changing professional workflows.

insights.claim: Amodo currently vibe-CADs very little of its work with its 60 mechanical, electronic, firmware and software engineers, but Milton expects per-engineer token spend to match software-company levels next year, and few of its engineers saturate premium subscriptions today.
insights.speaker: Tom Milton
insights.so_what: Hardware engineering is an upcoming source of token demand for AI labs.

insights.claim: PCB routing and similar hardware tasks look RL-friendly because they have verifiable rewards, so if labs hill-climb them, hardware engineering workflows could change quickly.
insights.speaker: Tom Milton
insights.so_what: Lab RL-environment investment in EDA and CAD tasks could rapidly lift capability and disrupt engineering services.

insights.claim: The key open question is hardware's equivalent of compilation and unit tests: either rapid physical prototyping with printers, CNC machines and robotic actuators, or simulations (finite element analysis, circuit simulators) good enough to cut physical builds; Amodo bets on rapid-turnaround prototyping, F1-style, and currently gives Claude control of 11 FDM 3D printers.
insights.speaker: Tom Milton
insights.so_what: Whether hardware AI progress comes via simulation or robotic labs determines who captures value (software tools vs prototyping and robotics).

insights.claim: Milton predicts AI will enable hardware customised for a customer base of one, citing a wake-light PCB he had Fable design in about 10 hours using Claude Code and KiCad, manufactured by a Chinese PCB fabricator, and a UWB cycling distance tracker.
insights.speaker: Tom Milton
insights.so_what: Lower hardware design cost expands long-tail hardware and strengthens PCB fabricators and component suppliers.

insights.claim: AI lets engineers cross disciplines: an Amodo mechanical engineer used Fable to design a PCB for a differential pressure sensor on an ARIA drone particle-sizer project, work that would normally take an electronics engineer a couple of hours.
insights.speaker: Tom Milton
insights.so_what: Productivity gains come first from collapsing handoffs between disciplines, not replacing specialists.

insights.claim: Safeguards for automated manufacturing are unclear: DNA synthesis screening offers a biology chokepoint, but 3D printers are abundant and easily hacked, and screening at the slicer would be easy to evade, so Milton does not endorse printer-level surveillance.
insights.speaker: Tom Milton
insights.so_what: Hardware misuse has no clear chokepoint, which complicates regulation of AI-enabled manufacturing.

themes.theme: R&D funding and the UK context

insights.claim: Amodo describes itself as a fit-for-purpose 'prime' (like Skunk Works or BBN) for turning philanthropic and government capital into catastrophic-risk hardware R&D, having delivered 100 hardware projects in about four years and sometimes delivering ARIA milestones 12 months early on 2 to 3 year projects.
insights.speaker: Tom Milton
insights.so_what: Execution capacity, not capital, is the bottleneck for philanthropy-funded science, favouring capable R&D contractors.

insights.claim: AI-lab-linked philanthropy (Anthropic Institute, Anthropic cofounders, OpenAI Foundation, Coefficient Giving) could give out tens of billions of dollars a year, with single-digit billions possibly spent on UK R&D, against UKRI's roughly 10 billion pounds a year.
insights.speaker: Tom Milton
insights.so_what: Philanthropic AI wealth may rival public science funders and reshape research funding allocation.

insights.claim: Government research funders like UKRI will struggle to adapt to AI-speed R&D, since five-year deliverables will shrink to months or weeks; Milton suggests shorter goals with frequent re-evaluation or large block grants, and R&D groups should run experiments in parallel since parallelism costs have fallen.
insights.speaker: Tom Milton
insights.so_what: Slow grant structures become a drag; flexible, fast-iteration funders and labs gain relative advantage.

insights.claim: Amodo is shifting from consultancy to a hardware R&D lab, taking on more upstream project selection and downstream spinouts as its engineering speeds up, with possible for-profit or nonprofit spinouts or open-sourcing.
insights.speaker: Tom Milton
insights.so_what: Faster engineering pushes services firms to capture more of the value chain.

insights.claim: Being bootstrapped in Sheffield gave Amodo underpriced engineering talent and insulation from the VC hype cycle, which Milton says would have prevented starting AI verification work.
insights.speaker: Tom Milton
insights.so_what: Location and funding structure shaped contrarian, mission-driven work that VC-backed peers would avoid.

insights.claim: When US export controls cut off access to Fable 5, Milton lost his AI-enabled electronics design capability overnight, illustrating the catastrophic dependence of non-US firms on frontier model access.
insights.speaker: Tom Milton
insights.so_what: Export controls on frontier models create supply risk for non-US AI-dependent businesses.

insights.claim: Milton expects a US compute crunch in which token demand exceeds supply, leading the US to prioritise domestic customers, and unless the UK has sovereign compute at high security level the US may be unwilling to export model weights, risking UK science, R&D and living standards.
insights.speaker: Tom Milton
insights.so_what: Supports demand for secure sovereign compute and data centres outside the US, and flags token-rationing risk.

insights.claim: Counterpoint: many tasks saturate at a certain intelligence level ('some problems are Sonnet problems'), so losing frontier access may matter less for some firms, though sovereign compute still has optionality and national security value, such as GCHQ-type analysis that would not run on a random foreign data centre.
insights.speaker: Tom Milton
insights.so_what: Not all AI demand requires frontier models; mid-tier model usage is more substitutable.
